Chapter Three: Building Trust and Facing Obstacles—Life Inside the Orphanage.
Living and working in the orphanage was a daily adventure, filled with challenges that tugged at both your heart and your patience. Imagine a house where every day feels a bit like a storm—there are arguments about chores, tears for parents who aren't there, and moments of laughter that can suddenly flip into frustration. The staff did their best to keep things running smoothly, offering comfort where they could, but it always felt like there was just one more need to fill.
Trust didn't come easy here. Many of these kids had learned the hard way not to rely on promises. When new volunteers showed up, you could feel the skepticism in the air. Building relationships meant showing up, day after day, with patience and a whole lot of little gestures—a shared joke, a hand with homework, or just listening when someone needed to talk. These small moments, believe it or not, were the real building blocks of trust.
I'll never forget one evening in the kitchen. A bunch of kids were helping with dinner—just peeling potatoes and stirring lentils, nothing fancy. But the energy was electric. Out of nowhere, a quiet girl started humming a song from her village. One by one, the others joined in, and suddenly the whole kitchen was filled with music and a feeling of belonging. For that moment, you could almost forget about the worries outside. It's amazing how healing can begin in such ordinary moments.
Still, the challenges never really disappeared. The orphanage was always short on essentials—food, clothes, even medicine. The building itself needed repairs, and there was always that nagging fear of eviction hanging over everyone. The staff pushed themselves to the limit, often putting the kids' needs ahead of their own. There was a strong sense of community, but the pressure was constant.
Beyond those walls, the world wasn’t any kinder. The city was changing, with the civil war bringing new waves of uncertainty. Every day, bits of bad news trickled in—violence, displacement, lost relatives. The kids worried about loved ones left behind, or villages that had disappeared. That sense of safety inside the orphanage? It was real, but it was also fragile. One rumor, one piece of bad news, and it could be shaken in an instant.
And yet, even with all that, there were moments of pure joy. Festivals lit up the orphanage with music, dancing, and shared meals. The kids created their own little traditions, finding ways to celebrate birthdays or just a good day at school. Every small victory—a new friend, a high grade—was met with genuine excitement. Their resilience was incredible. The way these kids held on to hope, even in the darkest times, was nothing short of inspiring.
Living that experience changed me. Sure, the work was exhausting, and there were days when it felt like too much. But the sense of purpose it brought? That was something special. The connections formed—between the kids, the staff, the volunteers—they became a kind of family. It stopped being just about seeing the world. It became about standing with people who needed you, about being part of a community that refused to give up, no matter what.
